It depends on what your endpoint calls, but FastAPI works either way. In any of the cases, FastAPI will still work asynchronously and be extremely fast.[1] But by following the guidelines, it will be able to do some performance optimizations.[1]

**Use `async def` if your libraries need `await`:**

```python
@app.get("/")
async def read_results():
    results = await some_library()
    return results
```

You can only use `await` inside of functions created with `async def`.[1]

**Use plain `def` if your library communicates with something (a database, an API, the file system, etc.)** and doesn't have support for using `await` (this is currently the case for most database libraries)[1]:

```python
@app.get("/")
def results():
    results = some_library()
    return results
```

**Other cases:**
- If your application (somehow) doesn't have to communicate with anything else and wait for it to respond, use `async def`, even if you don't need to use `await` inside.[1]
- If you just don't know, use normal `def`.[1]

**Why it matters:** When you declare a path operation function with normal `def` instead of `async def`, it is run in an external threadpool that is then awaited, instead of being called directly (as it would block the server).[2] For trivial compute-only functions, it's better to use `async def` unless your path operation functions use code that performs blocking I/O.[2]

You can also mix `def` and `async def` in your path operation functions as much as you need and define each one using the best option for you.[1] The same applies for dependencies. If a dependency is a standard `def` function instead of `async def`, it is run in the external threadpool.[2]

More details: https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/async/
